claim: Short-term (3 days) social isolation increases rates of social investigation in single-housed female mice during same-sex interactions compared to group-housed females.
source: In line with our previous behavioral findings (Zhao et al., 2021), we observed that single-housed female residents spent more time investigating visitors (Figure 1B; t-test, p=0.001)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant differences in investigation time between single-housed and group-housed females (p=0.001), with reference to Figure 1B showing the quantified data.

claim: Single-housed female mice mount female visitors during same-sex interactions, while group-housed females do not exhibit this behavior.
source: in many trials mounted visitors, a behavior that was not observed in group-housed residents (Figure 1C; 0 of 12 group-housed residents and 11 of 13 single-housed residents mounted visitors; z-test for independent proportions, p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1 for complete statistical details)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 0 of 12 group-housed residents mounted visitors while 11 of 13 single-housed residents did (p<0.001), with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Female pairs containing a single-housed resident produce higher rates of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) than pairs with a group-housed resident.
source: Female pairs that contained a single-housed resident also produced higher rates of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) than pairs with a group-housed resident (Figure 1D; Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant differences in USV rates (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.001), with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Single-housed females exhibit increased Fos expression in the preoptic area (POA) following same-sex social interactions compared to group-housed females.
source: Following social interactions with novel female visitors, single-housed females exhibited robust increases in Fos expression within the POA (Figure 1F, left; p<0.001) but not within the VMH (Figure 1F, middle; p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increases in POA Fos expression in single-housed females following social interactions (p<0.001), with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Baseline levels of Fos expression within the POA do not differ between group-housed and single-housed females that did not engage in social interactions.
source: These analyses revealed that baseline levels of Fos expression within the POA and the VMH did not differ between group-housed and single-housed females (Figure 1F, left and middle, open bars; two-way ANOVA to analyze Fos expression within each brain region, factor 1=housing status, factor 2=social interaction, followed by post-hoc Tukey's HSD tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests) showing no significant differences in baseline POA Fos expression between housing conditions, with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: POA Fos expression is positively correlated with the total amount of time spent in resident-initiated investigation for both group-housed and single-housed females.
source: POA Fos expression was significantly and positively correlated with the total amount of time spent in resident-initiated investigation for both group-housed and single-housed females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; linear regression, p<0.05)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (linear regression, p<0.05) showing significant positive correlation, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: POA Fos expression is positively correlated with the total time spent mounting by single-housed resident females.
source: as well as with the total time spent mounting by single-housed resident females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; p=0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p=0.01) showing significant positive correlation, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Single-housed females exhibit increased Fos expression in the caudolateral PAG following same-sex social interactions.
source: Similar to the POA, baseline Fos expression within the PAG did not differ between group-housed and single-housed females (p>0.05), and only single-housed females displayed increased PAG Fos expression following social interactions with novel female visitors (Figure 1F, right; p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increases in PAG Fos expression in single-housed females following social interactions (p<0.001), with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: The effects of short-term isolation on female social behavior are reversible following re-group-housing.
source: Following re-group-housing, time spent in social investigation and rates of USV production tended to decrease to pre-isolation levels (Figure 1G and I, top plots; p=0.08 for day 0 vs. day 17 investigation time and p=0.06 for day 0 vs. day 17 total USVs in re-group-housed females).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing trends toward return to baseline levels of social investigation and USV production after re-group-housing, with reference to Figure 1G and I.

claim: POA Fos expression is significantly lower in re-group-housed females relative to 17-day single-housed females following same-sex interactions.
source: Along with the attenuation of female social behaviors following re-group-housing, we also found that POA Fos expression was significantly lower in re-group-housed females relative to 17 day single-housed females (Figure 1J; t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant differences in POA Fos expression (t-test, p<0.001), with reference to Figure 1J.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons significantly reduces resident-initiated investigation in single-housed females.
source: Comparison of the social behaviors of single-housed females between CNO and saline sessions revealed that chemogenetic silencing of POAsocial neurons significantly reduced resident-initiated investigation (Figure 2B; n=17; red points; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in social investigation with CNO treatment (two-way ANOVA, p<0.01), with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons significantly reduces mounting in single-housed females.
source: Inhibition of POAsocial neurons also significantly reduced the proportion of females that exhibited mounting (Figure 2C; McNemar's test for paired proportions; p=0.04 for POAsocial CNO vs. saline).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in mounting with CNO treatment (McNemar's test, p=0.04), with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons significantly reduces USV production in single-housed females.
source: Finally, inhibition of POAsocial neurons significantly reduced USV production (Figure 2D; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in USV production with CNO treatment (two-way ANOVA, p<0.01), with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: CNO treatment does not affect social behaviors in control single-housed females with GFP expressed in POAsocial neurons.
source: In contrast, CNO treatment did not affect the production of any of these social behaviors in single-housed females with GFP expressed in POAsocial neurons (Figure 2B–D; n=14; black points; p>0.05 for all CNO vs. saline comparisons in the POAsocial-GFP control group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in social behaviors with CNO treatment in control animals (p>0.05), with reference to Figure 2B-D.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of neurons in the anterior hypothalamus (AH) or ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) does not affect social behaviors in single-housed females.
source: To investigate the specificity of these effects to chemogenetic silencing of POAsocial neurons, we also performed control experiments in which activity-dependent chemogenetic silencing in single-housed females was performed caudal to the POA within the anterior hypothalamus (AH; Figure 2B–D; n=12; brown points) or within the VMH (Figure 2B–D; n=5; gray points). No significant effects of CNO treatment on resident-initiated investigation, mounting, or total USVs were observed in these control groups (Figure 2C and D; p>0.05 for all).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant effects of CNO treatment in AH or VMH control groups (p>0.05), with reference to Figure 2B-D.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons does not affect overall movement in single-housed females.
source: The effect of chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons to decrease female social behavior also cannot be attributed to an overall decrease in movement (Figure 2E; paired t-test; p>0.5 for difference in movement between saline and CNO sessions; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant difference in movement between saline and CNO sessions (paired t-test, p>0.5), with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Caspase-mediated ablation of POAsocial neurons significantly reduces mounting in single-housed females.
source: Similar to the effects of chemogenetically inactivating POAsocial neurons, ablation of POAsocial neurons significantly reduced mounting in single-housed females (Figure 3C; McNemar's test for paired proportions; p=0.03 for proportion of trials with mounting on pre-4-OHT vs. post-4-OHT tests in POAsocial-caspase females; p>0.05 for pre-4-OHT vs. post-4-OHT in POAsocial-GFP females).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in mounting after ablation (McNemar's test, p=0.03), with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Caspase-mediated ablation of POAsocial neurons does not affect rates of social investigation in single-housed females.
source: In contrast to the effects of chemogenetic inhibition of POAsocial neurons, we found that caspase-mediated ablation of POAsocial neurons did not affect rates of social investigation in single-housed females, although both experimental and control females spent more time investigating visitors in the post-4-OHT session (Figure 3B; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p>0.05 for main effect of group, p<0.01 for main effect of time, p>0.05 for interaction effect).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant group effect on social investigation after ablation (two-way ANOVA, p>0.05 for main effect of group), with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Caspase-mediated ablation of POAsocial neurons does not reduce USV production in single-housed females.
source: Ablation of POAsocial neurons also failed to reduce USV production in pairs containing single-housed females (Figure 3D; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p>0.05 for pre-4-OHT vs. post-4-OHT total USVs in POAsocial-caspase females).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant reduction in USV production after ablation (two-way ANOVA, p>0.05), with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Ablation of POAsocial neurons in TRAP2 homozygous females significantly reduces mounting.
source: As in the original dataset, ablation of POAsocial neurons in TRAP2 homozygous females significantly reduced mounting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in mounting in TRAP2 homozygous females (p=0.04), with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ablation of POAsocial neurons reduces Fos expression in the POA to levels observed in females that did not engage in social interactions.
source: This analysis revealed that ablation of POAsocial neurons reduced Fos expression in the POA below the levels normally seen in either group-housed or single-housed females following same-sex interactions, down to levels observed in group-housed and single-housed females that were not given social interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; p<0.05 for POAsocial-caspase vs. group-housed and single-housed social interaction control groups; p>0.05 for POAsocial-caspase vs. group-housed and single-housed baseline control groups).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in POA Fos expression after ablation compared to social interaction controls (p<0.05), with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons elicits USV production in group-housed females during social sessions.
source: Interestingly, we found that when laser stimulation was applied during social sessions, optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons more readily elicited USV production than in solo sessions (Figure 4C; USVs elicited by blue laser stimulation in 8 of 9 POAsocial-ChR2 females; Mann Whitney U test performed on the difference in USV rates (laser - pre-laser), p=0.006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increase in USV production during laser stimulation in social sessions (Mann Whitney U test, p=0.006), with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons elicits higher rates of USVs when subject females are in close proximity to visitor females.
source: Moreover, optogenetic activation elicited higher rates of USVs when applied at times when subject females were in close proximity to visitor females (within 2 mouse body lengths) as compared to times when the females were farther apart (mean increase in USV rates from pre-laser to laser period was 2.96±2.32 USVs/s for 'near' stimulations, 1.84±1.75 USVs/s for 'far' stimulations; paired t-test performed on the difference in USV rates (laser - pre-laser) for 'far' vs. 'near' stimulations; p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant difference in USV elicitation based on proximity (paired t-test, p=0.02).

claim: Social investigation bouts that overlap with optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons are significantly longer than those without overlap.
source: This analysis revealed that social investigation bouts that overlapped with laser stimulation were significantly longer than those without overlap in POAsocial-ChR2 females but not in POAsocial-GFP females (Figure 4G; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p=0.001 for overlapping vs. non-overlapping for POAsocial-ChR2 females; p>0.05 for overlapping vs. non-overlapping for POAsocial-GFP females).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increase in bout duration during laser stimulation (two-way ANOVA, p=0.001), with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons does not reliably elicit mounting in group-housed females.
source: In contrast to the effects on USV production and social investigation, optogenetic activation of POAsocial neurons only infrequently elicited mounting (activation elicited 1 bout of mounting in n=1 POAsocial-ChR2 female and 0 bouts of mounting in the remaining n=8 POAsocial-ChR2 females).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mounting was elicited in only 1 of 9 POAsocial-ChR2 females.

claim: A majority of POAsocial neurons are GABAergic.
source: This analysis revealed that a majority of POAsocial neurons are GABAergic (Figure 6A and B; n=4, 76 ± 8.8%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing 76 ± 8.8% of Fos+ POA neurons co-expressed VGAT, with reference to Figure 6A and B.

claim: POAsocial neurons send axonal projections to the caudolateral PAG.
source: We next used the TRAP2 activity-dependent labeling strategy to express GFP in POAsocial neurons and found GFP-positive axons within the caudolateral PAG, indicating that at least some POAsocial neurons send axonal projections to the PAG (Figure 6C and D; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data showing GFP-positive axons in the PAG, with reference to Figure 6C and D.

claim: Approximately 20% of PAG-projecting POA neurons express Fos in single-housed females following same-sex interactions.
source: This experiment revealed that around 20% of PAG-projecting POA neurons express Fos in single-housed females following same-sex interactions (Figure 6E–G; n=4 females, percentage of tdTomato neurons that are Fos-positive=18.3 ± 2.9%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing combined with Fos immunostaining showing 18.3 ± 2.9% overlap, with reference to Figure 6E-G.

claim: Short-term isolation exerts larger effects on male social behavior during opposite-sex interactions relative to same-sex interactions.
source: The finding that short-term isolation exerts larger effects on male social behavior during subsequent opposite-sex interactions relative to same-sex interactions is consistent with prior work (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing context-dependent effects of isolation on male behavior, with citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2021).

claim: Single-housed males spend more time investigating visitors than group-housed males.
source: With respect to resident-initiated investigation, we found significant main effects of both housing and social context: single-housed males spent more time investigating visitors than group-housed males, and males spent more time investigating female visitors than male visitors (Figure 7A; two-way ANOVA, p=0.02 for main effect of housing; p<0.001 for main effect of social context; p>0.05 for interaction effect).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant main effect of housing on investigation time (two-way ANOVA, p=0.02), with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: Single-housed males are more likely than group-housed males to mount female visitors.
source: With respect to mounting, we found that single-housed males were more likely than group-housed males to mount female visitors, but the proportion of trials with mounting did not differ for single-housed males vs. group-housed males during male-male interactions (Figure 7B; z-tests for independent proportions; p=0.046 for group-housed vs. single-housed with female visitor, p>0.05 for group-housed vs. single-housed with male visitor).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant difference in mounting during male-female interactions (z-test, p=0.046), with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Single-housed males that interact with female visitors exhibit increased USV production relative to group-housed males.
source: Similarly, there was a context-dependent effect of social isolation on male USV production, whereby only single-housed males that interacted with female visitors exhibited increased USV production relative to group-housed males (Figure 7C; two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey's HSD tests; p<0.001 for total USVs in single-housed MF vs. group-housed MF trials; p>0.05 for total USVs in single-housed MM vs. group-housed MM trials).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increase in USV production in single-housed males during male-female interactions (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.001), with reference to Figure 7C.

claim: POA Fos expression is significantly elevated in single-housed males following interactions with females relative to other groups.
source: When we examined POA Fos expression in these four groups of males, we found that POA Fos was significantly elevated in single-housed males following interactions with females relative to the other three groups (Figure 7D; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post-hoc HSD tests; p<0.05 for difference in POA Fos between single-housed MF and all other groups).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant elevation in POA Fos expression in single-housed males after male-female interactions (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.05), with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of male POAsocial neurons significantly reduces mounting during interactions with females.
source: As in females, chemogenetic inhibition of male POAsocial neurons significantly reduced the proportion of trials with mounting (Figure 7G; z-test for difference between proportions; p=0.04 for proportion of trials with mounting on CNO vs. saline days in POAsocial-hM4Di males; p>0.05 for proportion of trials with mounting on CNO vs. saline days in POAsocial-GFP males).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in mounting with CNO treatment (z-test, p=0.04), with reference to Figure 7G.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of male POAsocial neurons does not alter rates of resident-initiated social investigation.
source: In contrast to our findings in females, chemogenetic inhibition of male POAsocial neurons did not alter rates of resident-initiated social investigation (Figure 7F; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p<0.001 for main effect of group; p>0.05 for main effect of drug and for interaction effect)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant effect of drug treatment on social investigation (two-way ANOVA, p>0.05 for main effect of drug), with reference to Figure 7F.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of male POAsocial neurons does not affect total USVs.
source: and also did not affect total USVs (Figure 7H; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor; p>0.05 for main effects and interaction effect).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant effects on USV production (two-way ANOVA, p>0.05), with reference to Figure 7H.

claim: POAsocial-hM4Di males spent significantly more time mounting female visitors during TRAPing sessions than POAsocial-hM4Di females.
source: Interestingly, we found that POAsocial-hM4Di males spent significantly more time mounting female visitors during TRAPing sessions than POAsocial-hM4Di females (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Mann Whitney U test; p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant sex difference in mounting time during TRAPing sessions (Mann Whitney U test, p=0.004), with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Long-term isolation can lead to the emergence of anti-social behaviors in both humans and rodents.
source: While long-term isolation can lead to the emergence of anti-social behaviors in both humans and rodents (An et al., 2017; Arrigo and Bullock, 2008; Check et al., 1985; Hossain et al., 2020; Killgore et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2022; Machimbarrena et al., 2019; Matsumoto et al., 2005; Mears and Bales, 2009; Reid et al., 2022; Toth et al., 2011; Valzelli, 1973; Weiss et al., 2004; Wiberg and Grice, 1963; Zelikowsky et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on long-term isolation effects.

claim: Short-term isolation typically increases levels of social motivation and promotes social-seeking behaviors.
source: short-term isolation typically increases levels of social motivation and promotes social-seeking behaviors (Baumeister and Leary, 1995; Cacioppo et al., 2006; Cacioppo and Cacioppo, 2018; House et al., 1988; Lee et al., 2021; Niesink and van Ree, 1982; Panksepp and Beatty, 1980; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on short-term isolation effects.

claim: The mesolimbic pathway plays an important role in regulating social motivation and social reward.
source: The mesolimbic pathway (i.e. projections from dopaminergic ventral tegmental neurons to the ventral striatum) plays an important role in regulating social motivation and social reward, during courtship as well as during same-sex interactions (Bariselli et al., 2018; Dai et al., 2022; Dölen et al., 2013; Gunaydin et al., 2014; Hung et al., 2017; Love, 2014; Melis et al., 2022; Resendez et al., 2020; Robinson et al., 2011; Solié et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2014; Walum and Young, 2018; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on mesolimbic pathway function.

claim: Changes in the function of the mesolimbic pathway have been reported following long-term social isolation.
source: In line with its role in regulating social behavior, changes in the function of the mesolimbic pathway have been reported following long-term (weeks-long) social isolation and/or early-life social isolation (McWain et al., 2022; Musardo et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2021; Yorgason et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on mesolimbic pathway changes after isolation.

claim: Short-term isolation in adult animals has been shown to affect midbrain dopamine neurons in humans and rodents.
source: The neural circuit changes that mediate the effects of short-term isolation on social behavior in adult animals are comparatively less explored, but here as well, recent studies in both humans and rodents have implicated changes in various populations of midbrain dopamine neurons (Inagaki et al., 2016; Matthews et al., 2016; Tomova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on short-term isolation effects on dopamine neurons.

claim: The POA has been implicated in regulating social approach in mice.
source: Given the robust effects of short-term isolation on these three aspects of female social behavior, we focused our analyses on two hypothalamic regions implicated in regulating these behaviors: the preoptic area (POA), which regulates social approach (McHenry et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (McHenry et al., 2017).

claim: The POA has been implicated in regulating social reward in mice.
source: the preoptic area (POA), which regulates social approach (McHenry et al., 2017), social reward (Hu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Hu et al., 2021).

claim: The POA has been implicated in regulating mounting behavior in mice.
source: the preoptic area (POA), which regulates social approach (McHenry et al., 2017), social reward (Hu et al., 2021), mounting (Floody, 1989; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Floody, 1989; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018).

claim: The POA has been implicated in regulating USV production in mice.
source: the preoptic area (POA), which regulates social approach (McHenry et al., 2017), social reward (Hu et al., 2021), mounting (Floody, 1989; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018) and USV production (Chen et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2019; Green et al., 2018; Karigo et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Chen et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2019; Green et al., 2018; Karigo et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020).

claim: The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) regulates mounting behavior in mice.
source: and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), which regulates mounting (Hashikawa et al., 2017; Karigo et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Hashikawa et al., 2017; Karigo et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2022).

claim: The caudolateral PAG plays a well-established role in the control of vocalization in vertebrates and USV production in mice.
source: We also examined Fos expression within the caudolateral periaqueductal gray (PAG), based on the well-established role of this region in the control of vocalization in vertebrates and USV production in mice (Chen et al., 2021; Jürgens, 1994; Michael et al., 2020; Tschida et al., 2019; Ziobro et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Chen et al., 2021; Jürgens, 1994; Michael et al., 2020; Tschida et al., 2019; Ziobro et al., 2024).

claim: The POA has been implicated in the regulation of male sexual behavior, including courtship vocalizations in rodents and birds.
source: An extensive body of past work has implicated the POA in the regulation of male sexual behavior, including in the regulation of male courtship vocalizations in both rodents and birds (Alger and Riters, 2006; Bean et al., 1981; Gao et al., 2019; Merari and Ginton, 1975; Riters, 2012; Riters et al., 2000; Riters and Ball, 1999; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on POA function in male sexual behavior.

claim: Activation of genetically-defined subsets of POA neurons can elicit USV production in both male and female mice.
source: Past work has also shown that activation of genetically-defined subsets of POA can elicit the production of USVs in both male and female mice (Chen et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2019; Karigo et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on POA activation and USV production.

claim: POAsocial neurons may promote USV production via disinhibition of PAG-USV neurons.
source: Our retrograde and anterograde tracing experiments demonstrate that at least a subset of POAsocial neurons project to the caudolateral PAG where neurons important for USV production reside, and an attractive possibility is that POAsocial neurons promote USV production via disinhibition of PAG-USV neurons as previously demonstrated for genetically-defined subsets of POA neurons (Chen et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020; Tschida et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data from the current study and citations to prior research on POA-PAG circuits (Chen et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020; Tschida et al., 2019).

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tacr1+ POA neurons elicits both mounting and USV production in male mice.
source: A recent study found that optogenetic activation of Tacr1+ POA neurons elicits both mounting and USV production in male mice and that optogenetic activation of the axon terminals of these neurons within the PAG also promotes mounting, suggesting that some POA neurons may regulate the production of multiple social behaviors (Bayless et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Bayless et al., 2023).

claim: Distinct subsets of male Esr1+ POA neurons exhibit selective tuning in their neuronal activity to sniffing vs. mounting during interactions with females.
source: However, another study found that distinct subsets of male Esr1+ POA neurons exhibit selective tuning in their neuronal activity to sniffing vs. mounting during interactions with females (Yang et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Yang et al., 2023).

claim: Projection-defined subsets of galanin-expressing POA neurons regulate different aspects of parental behavior.
source: The latter organization would be reminiscent of how projection-defined subsets of galanin-expressing POA neurons regulate different aspects of parental behavior (Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Kohl et al., 2018).

claim: Prior studies reported effects on both mounting and USV production following reversible manipulations of POA activity.
source: These differences are largely consistent with prior studies that reported effects on both mounting and USV production following reversible manipulations of POA activity and effects on mounting but not on USV production following irreversible manipulations of POA activity (Bean et al., 1981; Chen et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2019; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on POA manipulations.

claim: Reversible silencing of motor cortex disrupted performance of a learned forelimb reaching task in rats, while permanent lesions had no effect after learning.
source: Such a relationship was demonstrated for motor cortex, whereby reversible silencing of motor cortex disrupted performance of a learned forelimb reaching task in rats, while permanent lesions of motor cortex had no effect on task performance after learning (Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Otchy et al., 2015).

claim: The VMH regulates male mounting behavior during interactions with other males.
source: Although the POA plays a well-established role in the regulation of mounting behavior by male rodents during interactions with females, interactions which are typically marked by high rates of USV production and are considered affiliative, the authors found that the VMH regulates male mounting behavior during interactions with other males, which is typically not accompanied by USV production and often precedes fighting.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Karigo et al., 2021.

claim: Previous studies that elicited mounting in male mice via optogenetic activation of POA neurons used longer laser stimulation trains (15-30 s) than employed in the current study.
source: We note that previous studies that elicited mounting in male mice via optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA neurons, Tacr1+ POA neurons, or POA neurons that co-express Esr1 and VGAT used longer laser stimulation trains (15–30 s) than we employed in the current study (Bayless et al., 2023; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Bayless et al., 2023; Karigo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2018).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition or optogenetic inhibition of Esr1+ POA neurons reduces USV production in male mice.
source: These findings differ also from recent work showing that chemogenetic inhibition (Chen et al., 2021) or optogenetic inhibition (Karigo et al., 2021) of Esr1+ POA neurons reduces USV production in male mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Chen et al., 2021; Karigo et al., 2021).

claim: The POA regulates social behavior in both females and males, including in non-sexual social contexts.
source: The current study adds to an emerging body of literature implicating the POA in the regulation of social behavior in both females and males, including in non-sexual social contexts (Fukumitsu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; McHenry et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on POA function in social behavior.

claim: Reunion with same-sex cagemates following short-term somatic isolation increases the activity of calcitonin-receptor (Calcr) expressing POA neurons in BALB/c mice.
source: A recent study using BALB/c mice found that reunion with same-sex cagemates following short-term 'somatic isolation' (i.e. separation from cagemates via a partition that permits visual, auditory, and olfactory signaling but prevents physical contact) increases the activity of calcitonin-receptor (Calcr) expressing POA neurons (Fukumitsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Fukumitsu et al., 2023).

claim: Knockdown of Calcr expression in POA neurons reduced social-seeking behaviors directed at the cage partition exhibited by single-housed females.
source: Knockdown of Calcr expression in these neurons reduced social-seeking behaviors directed at the cage partition exhibited by single-housed females, and chemogenetic activation of these neurons increased partition-biting behavior in single-housed females.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Fukumitsu et al., 2023.

claim: Optogenetic activation of MPNreunion neurons during reunion with cagemates following short-term social isolation decreased social investigation in FVB/NJ female mice.
source: Another recent study using female FVB/NJ mice applied a TRAP2-based intersectional approach to identify POA neurons that increase their activity following reunion with same-sex cagemates (MPNreunion neurons; Liu et al., 2023). Optogenetic activation of these neurons did not alter social investigation in group-housed females, whereas activation of these neurons during reunion with cagemates following short-term social isolation decreased social investigation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Liu et al., 2023).

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of MPNreunion neurons during reunion did not alter rates of social investigation in single-housed females.
source: However, optogenetic inhibition of MPNreunion during reunion did not alter rates of social investigation in single-housed females.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Liu et al., 2023.

claim: Alterations in social behavior are characteristic of many neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder.
source: Alterations in social behavior are characteristic of many neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder (Chevallier et al., 2012; Clements et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Chevallier et al., 2012; Clements et al., 2018).

claim: Either female in a dyad can produce USVs during female-female interactions.
source: Although either female in a dyad can produce USVs (Warren et al., 2020), the robust effects of short-term isolation on the non-vocal social behaviors of single-housed females suggest that at least some of the elevation in total USVs is driven by increased USV production by the single-housed resident.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Warren et al., 2020) and inference from current behavioral data.

claim: The robust triad of changes in social behavior exhibited by C57BL/6 J females following short-term isolation affords a powerful opportunity to investigate neural circuit mechanisms.
source: Although some studies of social isolation have avoided the use of C57BL/6 J female mice, the robust triad of changes in social behavior exhibited by these females following short-term isolation affords a powerful opportunity to continue investigating neural circuit mechanisms through which short-term social isolation promotes social behaviors
evidence: Based on the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings showing robust behavioral changes in C57BL/6 J females.

claim: POAsocial neurons promote social behaviors in single-housed mice in a manner that depends on sex and social context.
source: Together, these experiments identify a population of preoptic hypothalamic neurons that promote social behaviors in single-housed mice in a manner that depends on sex and social context.
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data from chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations in males and females across different social contexts.

claim: The POA regulates the production of USVs by single-housed females engaged in same-sex interactions.
source: In the current study, we demonstrate that reversible silencing of POA neurons that increase their activity during same-sex interactions decreases female USV production, indicating that the POA regulates the production of USVs by single-housed females engaged in same-sex interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing chemogenetic silencing of POAsocial neurons reduces USV production.

claim: The POA regulates mounting behavior in both male and female mice that is directed toward female social partners and is accompanied by USV production.
source: Taken together with the findings of the current study, we conclude that the POA regulates mounting behavior in both male and female mice that is directed toward female social partners and is accompanied by USV production.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the current study and integration with prior research findings (Karigo et al., 2021).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POA neurons in single-housed females reduces all three measured social behaviors (investigation, mounting, and USV production).
source: We found that chemogenetic inactivation of POA neurons in single-housed females dramatically reduced all three behaviors (Figure 5M–O; paired t-tests, p<0.05 for all behaviors).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using non-Cre-dependent chemogenetic silencing showing significant reductions in all behaviors (paired t-tests, p<0.05), with reference to Figure 5M-O.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of POA neurons in group-housed females significantly reduces USV production during same-sex interactions.
source: Notably, we found that although rates of USV production were quite low, chemogenetic inhibition of POA neurons significantly reduced total USVs produced during same-sex interactions between group-housed females (Figure 5L; paired t-test, p=0.048).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reduction in USV production with CNO treatment (paired t-test, p=0.048), with reference to Figure 5L.
